idiom_name: scope struct with a parent pointer and a per-scope entry table, plus define/lookup functions
implementation_notes: C ships no symbol-table or name-lookup primitive, so the classic structure is written out in full: a scope object holding an entry array or a chained hash table plus a pointer to its enclosing scope, a current-scope pointer, and the operations scope-open, scope-close, define (rejecting a duplicate in the current scope) and lookup (walking the parent chain from the innermost scope outward). What replaces the OO structure is convention plus ownership discipline: st_insert/st_lookup-style helpers fill the roles, and scopes and symbols are allocated in the same arena as the AST nodes so that symbols stay valid for later passes; the standard designs are the cactus stack of per-scope hash tables and Louden's Tiny-compiler symtab. Keep the hand-written form - C is the language in which these tables are normally implemented, and the classic structure stays justified whenever the front end is a compiler rather than a one-shot analysis; a single global table with a scope tag is only worth considering when per-scope allocation shows up in profiles.
pitfalls: Scope and symbol lifetime: freeing a scope when it closes invalidates every symbol that AST nodes and later phases still point to - allocate symbols in one arena and free only per compilation.

A per-scope hash table costs an allocation per block; if lookup is a linear scan over a linked list instead, a deeply nested file with many names degrades towards quadratic parsing - hash or intern names once.

The duplicate check must be local to the innermost scope: scanning the whole chain before inserting turns legal shadowing into a spurious redeclaration error, and skipping the check lets an inner declaration silently replace the outer one.
